title: Williamsburg, Virginia
seoTitle: Charter Bus to Williamsburg, Virginia: Group Guide
excerpt: A charter bus to Williamsburg, Virginia covers the whole Historic Triangle. What to see, which vehicle fits, and the parkway routing that catches coaches out.

heroImage.alt: Costumed interpreters and colonial buildings along Duke of Gloucester Street in Colonial Williamsburg

extraImage.alt: The Governor's Palace and its formal gardens in Colonial Williamsburg

body.text: Colonial Williamsburg is 301 acres of restored and reconstructed eighteenth-century town, staffed by people who will stay in character while you ask them about the price of nails. It is the largest living history museum in the country and it works exceptionally well for groups. A charter bus to Williamsburg is also the practical choice, because the sites worth seeing are spread across three separate towns.
The Historic Triangle is three destinations, not one

Williamsburg, Jamestown and Yorktown sit within about twenty miles of each other and together tell one continuous story: the first permanent English settlement, the colonial capital, and the siege that ended the Revolution. Most groups that come for Williamsburg alone end up wishing they had planned for all three.

items: Colonial Williamsburg: Duke of Gloucester Street, the Governor's Palace, the Capitol, and the trade shops where blacksmiths, coopers and printers work with period tools. A full day on its own.
Jamestown Settlement: a re-created fort, a Powhatan village and full-scale replicas of the three ships that arrived in 1607. Half a day, and the strongest stop for younger students.
Historic Jamestowne: the actual archaeological site, separate from the settlement museum and often confused with it. Book the right one.
Yorktown Battlefield and the American Revolution Museum: where Cornwallis surrendered in 1781, with earthworks you can walk.

body.text: The routing detail that catches coaches out

The Colonial Parkway is the scenic road linking the three sites, and it carries restrictions on commercial traffic. A charter operator needs to know that before the day rather than at the entrance, and the alternative routes on Route 60 and the Colonial Parkway's parallel roads add time to the schedule.

Ask your operator directly how they intend to route between Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown. It is a fair question, the answer takes ten seconds, and it separates operators who have run the Triangle from those who have looked at a map.
Buying tickets, and the mistake groups make

Colonial Williamsburg's streets are free to walk. Admission buys entry to the exhibition buildings, the trade shops and the programs, which is the actual content. A group that arrives without tickets can wander a pretty street and see very little of what it came for.

Group rates exist and must be arranged in advance. Combination tickets covering Jamestown Settlement and the Yorktown museum are the better value if you are doing more than one site, and they need booking ahead too.
Which charter bus suits a Williamsburg trip

items: Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is the standard school-group vehicle, with designated coach parking at the visitor center and the Jamestown and Yorktown sites.
Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) suits a smaller class or a senior group and moves more easily between the three towns.
Twenty-eight to sixty: a [school bus](/fleet/school-buses) is economical for Virginia districts within about two hours.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) works for a family reunion or a small historical society.

The walking is the part groups underestimate

Duke of Gloucester Street alone is about a mile end to end, and a full day in the historic area routinely puts five or six miles on everybody's feet, much of it on uneven brick and gravel. For a senior group, plan around the shuttle buses that run within the historic area and pick a smaller number of buildings.

Summer heat compounds it. Virginia in July is hot and humid, the historic area has limited shade, and interpreters in wool coats are doing it harder than you are. An early start and a long midday break works far better than pushing through.
Getting there

[Williamsburg](/locations/virginia/williamsburg) sits between [Richmond](/locations/virginia/richmond), about an hour west, and [Norfolk](/locations/virginia/norfolk), around fifty minutes south-east. Washington is two and a half to three hours north on Interstate 95, which is why so many school groups come down for two days rather than one. We also run pickups from [Newport News](/locations/virginia/newport-news), [Hampton](/locations/virginia/hampton) and [Yorktown](/locations/virginia/yorktown).

Groups searching for charter bus rental near me for a spring Williamsburg trip should book early. April and May are the peak school weeks and vehicles across the whole mid-Atlantic tighten considerably.
When to go

April, May, September and October are the best months: mild, green, and with every program running. Summer is hot but the full living-history schedule is in operation and the evening programs are excellent. December is the quiet favorite — Grand Illumination and candlelit streets make it the most atmospheric time of year, and the crowds are far lighter than in spring.
